Fit a Bayesian multivariate state-space model

Source: R/mvgam_core.R
mvgam.Rd

Fits the model in Stan. The observation formula takes brms syntax, and trend_formula adds a latent dynamic process, such as a random walk or an autoregression, with predictors of its own. A list of multiply imputed data frames fits the model to each frame and pools the draws.

Usage

mvgam(
  formula,
  trend_formula = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  newdata = NULL,
  trend_map = NULL,
  loadings_prior = NULL,
  backend = getOption("brms.backend", "cmdstanr"),
  combine = TRUE,
  family = gaussian(),
  threads = NULL,
  save_pars = brms::save_pars(),
  run_model = TRUE,
  ...
)

Arguments

formula

Main observation model formula (supports brms syntax). Smooth specials s(), t2(), gp(), varying intercepts and slopes, monotonic mo(), measurement-error me(), distributional dpar sub-formulas and offset() are all available. gp() accepts both the approximate Hilbert-space form (gp(x, k = 20)) and the exact full-covariance form (gp(x), no k). Prediction at newdata requires the approximate form. An exact gp() term fits and scores in-sample. mvgam() says so once per session.

trend_formula

A one-sided formula for the latent process: a trend constructor such as AR() with any predictors of the latent state. Write lv_axis() in a term to vary its effect by latent factor, or by series in a model without factors, as in ~ x:lv_axis() + AR(). The series column itself is not supported in a term of this formula. An exact gp() term here also predicts in-sample alone. Forecasting a model that holds one requires the approximate form.

data

Data frame, or a list of multiply imputed data frames or a mids object from mice. mvgam_multiple() describes the imputation path.

newdata

Optional held-out data.frame, stored on the fit as object$test_data. forecast() forecasts to it when called without newdata. plot(fit, type = "series") overlays it. The fit itself draws no forecasts. forecast() propagates the fitted latent state forward in time per posterior draw. posterior_predict(mod, newdata = mod$test_data) marginalises over the trend's stochastic dynamics at the supplied design points. Use forecast() for time-series forecasting and posterior_predict() for marginal predictive checks.

trend_map

Optional fixed factor loadings, in one of three forms:

  • a numeric n_series x n_lv matrix of loadings. NA entries are sampled. Finite entries stay fixed on Z in the posterior. An all-NA matrix fixes nothing and acts as trend_map = NULL

  • a data.frame(series, trend) assigning each series to one latent process

  • "identity", one process per series, or "shared", one process for every series

A factor model without a trend_map samples every loading. It identifies Z after sampling by a thin QR rotation (Heaps and Jermyn 2024). A trend_map with any fixed entry takes no rotation. The argument requires a trend_formula. It is an alternative to the trend_map argument of the trend constructor, and supplying both is an error. loadings_prior lists the trend_map forms a structured loadings prior accepts.

loadings_prior

Optional named list specifying a structured prior on the unconstrained factor loadings matrix following Heaps & Jermyn (2024). The loadings belong to a trend with latent factors. The argument requires a trend_formula. Supplying it without one is an error. When supplied, the default iid to_vector(Z) ~ student_t(3, 0, 0.5) prior is replaced with a per-column matrix-normal prior of the form Z[, i] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(0, L_Phi), where the among-row scale matrix Phi is assembled multiplicatively from any combination of:

  • a per-series feature matrix (features), expanded into an ARD exponential kernel via gp_exponential_cov()

  • one or more pairwise distance matrices (distances), each contributing an exp(-d / theta) factor

Accepted fields:

  • features: string lookup into data2, a numeric matrix, or a data.frame. Columns are encoded by type (numeric/integer/logical: z-score; ordered factor: z-score after as.numeric(); unordered factor / character: one-hot with all levels retained, following Heaps Sect. 6.2). Each encoded column receives its own ARD length-scale.

  • distances: string name (or character vector of names) of pairwise distance matrices in data2, or a single matrix / named list of matrices passed inline. Each matrix is rescaled to maximum entry one so the default length-scale prior is interpretable on a unit scale (matching Heaps Supps S4.2.1).

  • column_shrinkage: "iid" (default; no shrinkage) or "mgp" (multiplicative-gamma-process increasing shrinkage of Bhattacharya & Dunson 2011, used in Heaps Eq. (9)). "mgp" applies its column scale through the shared innovation scale. It is available for AR(), RW() and ZMVN() trends. VAR() builds its own innovation covariance and has no shared scale for it; pair a VAR() factor model with "iid" instead.

  • mgp_a1, mgp_a2: numeric MGP hyperparameters, only used when column_shrinkage = "mgp". Default (2, 4) lies within the a2 in [3, 5] range recommended for moderate-n ecology / community panels by Legramanti, Durante and Dunson (2020, JRSS-B) and Schiavon, Canale and Dunson (2022, Biometrics 78:995). Heaps Sect. 6.3.1 used (2, 3) for the gas-demand application; Sect. 6.2.2 used (2, 6) for the Finnish-bird JSDM. Lower a2 for less shrinkage when the data weakly identify the active rank.

Length-scales receive a lognormal(0, 1) prior in the model block. This prior is set on the standardised distance scale. Pairwise distance matrices are rescaled to max(d) = 1 inside the normaliser. A length-scale of 1 then corresponds to correlation exp(-1) between the two most distant series. Heaps' Finnish-birds application (Sect. 6.2.2) used the wider lognormal(0, sqrt(10)) instead; override the default by passing a prior() for theta_features / theta_dist_<name> if your data weakly identify length-scales and you want less regularisation. Note: the max(d) = 1 rule is the natural generic standardisation. Heaps Supps S4.2.1 used "root-to-tip distance = 1" for ultrametric phylogenies, which corresponds to max(d) = 2 (twice the per-leaf depth); pre-standardise your distance matrix to match if exact parity matters. Identification. The structured prior applies to the sampled columns of Z. Where the QR rotation gives the reported loadings Z_tilde, each of its columns mixes the sampled columns. shared_variation() and residual_cor() use Z Z', which is the same before and after the rotation. See the Identification section of the trend constructors.

Compatibility with trend_map:

  • trend_map = NULL (default): compatible. n_lv alone triggers the free-Z factor model; loadings_prior applies to the sampled Z column-wise.

  • trend_map = matrix(NA_real_, n_series, n_lv) (all-NA mask, used internally by jsdgam()): compatible. Treated as a free-Z trigger upstream; loadings_prior applies as if trend_map were NULL.

  • trend_map with a mix of fixed entries and NAs: incompatible. Partial-Z parameterises the free entries as a vector under an iid student_t(3, 0, 1) prior, which would overlap with the matrix-normal structure and double-count regularisation.

  • Fully-fixed trend_map (no NAs): incompatible. The structured prior has no free parameters to act on.

backend

"cmdstanr" or "rstan". Defaults to getOption("brms.backend", "cmdstanr").

combine

Logical. With imputed data, TRUE (default) pools the imputation fits into one and FALSE returns them as a list.

family

A description of the response distribution and link function, given as a family function, a call to one or its name. Supports most brms families, including the ordinal families (brms::cumulative(), brms::sratio(), brms::cratio(), brms::acat()). The brms families needing a separate linear predictor per response category, brms::categorical(), brms::multinomial() and brms::dirichlet(), are refused: use categ(), multi() and diri(), which take the categories in long format and share one latent structure across them. A family whose mean has to stay positive needs a link that keeps it there once a trend enters the linear predictor: pair stats::Gamma(), brms::weibull(), brms::exponential(), brms::frechet() and stats::inverse.gaussian() with link = "log". Their default links leave the mean positive only where the predictor is. A latent trend is centred near zero and reaches negative values, where the likelihood is undefined. mvgam() warns before fitting. brms::lognormal() is the exception: its mu is a log-scale location that takes any sign.

A family written inside a univariate brms::bf() is the model's family, as in brms. In a multivariate model each response may take its own family, in which case name it inside that response's brms::bf(): bf(count ~ x, family = poisson()) + bf(seen ~ x, family = bernoulli()). Passing a list of families to this argument, as brms::brm() allows, is not supported; the family belongs to the response that names it. A single family given here applies to every response that does not name one of its own. Closure-unit and multi-response families (occ(), nmix(), mvn(), mvt(), diri(), multi(), categ()) lay their data out by unit. Each models its response alone and cannot be one response of a multivariate model.

threads

Positive integer number of threads per chain, or NULL (the default) for none. The model is compiled with cpp_options$stan_threads = TRUE. cmdstanr then samples with threads_per_chain = threads. The closure-unit families (nmix(), occ()) and the multi-response families (diri(), mvn(), mvt(), multi(), categ()) split their likelihood over units with reduce_sum, in about eight chunks. With 50 or more closure units, threads = 4 samples about a third faster. Fewer units can sample slower, the threading overhead outweighing the gain. A brms family without a trend_formula uses the threading brms writes.

A brms-native family with a trend_formula samples serially whatever threads says. When it threads, brms moves the mu assignment inside partial_log_lik_lpmf, where mvgam cannot add the trend to it. The program is then built without threading. This applies to every trend model under a brms-native family: RW(), AR(), VAR(), LLT(), ZMVN(), CAR() and PW(). Each fit that drops the request warns. A batch script that fits repeatedly shows it every time.

save_pars

A brms::save_pars() object naming which parameters the posterior keeps. A model is built from working variables it also reports under another name: the standardised deviates a group-level block is scaled from, the unscaled coefficients a shrinkage prior scales, the ordered intercepts a mixture is identified by. Those are left out by default, as brms leaves them out. save_pars(all = TRUE) keeps every one. group and latent keep the per-level deviations and the latent values of a me() covariate. manual names individual parameters to keep.

run_model

Logical. FALSE builds the model without parsing, compiling or sampling it. The result holds $stancode, $standata and the prior table, with $fit set to NULL. stancode.mvgam_formula(), standata.mvgam_formula() and get_prior.mvgam_formula() return them. Methods that need draws, such as summary() and forecast(), refuse it. A jsdgam() model has no mvgam_formula(), which makes run_model = FALSE the way to inspect one before fitting. Defaults to TRUE.

...

Further arguments for the model and its sampler.

prior takes a brmsprior built with brms::prior(). Its rows replace the matching defaults. get_prior.mvgam_formula() lists every class a model takes, with trend classes carrying a _trend suffix. The plural priors is accepted as well.

chains, iter, warmup, thin, seed and control reach Stan as in brms::brm(). cores sets how many chains sample at once. It defaults to getOption("mc.cores") when that option is set and otherwise to one fewer than the machine's cores, up to chains.

algorithm selects how the posterior is explored. It accepts "sampling" (the default), "meanfield", "fullrank" or "fixed_param" on either backend, plus "pathfinder" and "laplace" when backend = "cmdstanr".

init sets the starting values. It accepts "random" (the default), "0", a numeric value, a list or a function. With backend = "cmdstanr" it also accepts "pathfinder". That keyword runs Stan's Pathfinder approximation on the compiled model and draws one starting value per chain from it. The requested algorithm still explores the posterior. The fit stays exact. It helps a model whose chains stall at a poor starting point or fill warmup with divergences. On a model that already warms up cleanly it adds about a second and lowers effective samples per second.

Five arguments shape the Stan program and reach brms unchanged:

  • knots gives knot positions by covariate name, for the observation and trend formulas alike.

  • drop_unused_levels decides whether a factor level with no observations still takes a coefficient.

  • sample_prior takes "no", "yes" or "only". Under "only" the observation likelihood drops out and the latent process keeps its prior. The draws then show what the model implies before any response is observed.

  • normalize = FALSE drops the normalising constants from the sampling statements. Sampling is faster and the posterior is unchanged.

  • save_model names a file to write the Stan program to.

Value

An object of class mvgam.

References

Clark, N. J. and Wells, K. (2023). Dynamic Generalized Additive Models for forecasting discrete ecological time series. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 14:771-784. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13974

Burkner, P.-C. (2017). brms: An R package for Bayesian multilevel models using Stan. Journal of Statistical Software, 80(1):1-28. doi:10.18637/jss.v080.i01

Wood, S. N. (2017). Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R (2nd edition). Chapman and Hall/CRC.

Heaps, S. E. and Jermyn, I. H. (2024). Structured prior distributions for the covariance matrix in latent factor models. Statistics and Computing, 34:143. doi:10.1007/s11222-024-10454-0 (post-hoc QR identification of latent factor loadings; structured loadings_prior construction.)

Riutort-Mayol, G., Burkner, P.-C., Andersen, M. R., Solin, A. and Vehtari, A. (2023). Practical Hilbert space approximate Bayesian Gaussian processes for probabilistic programming. Statistics and Computing, 33:1. doi:10.1007/s11222-022-10167-2 (used when formula or trend_formula contains gp() terms.)

See also

trend_constructors lists the latent trends. mvgam_families lists the observation families mvgam adds to those of brms. how_to_cite() writes a methods paragraph for a fitted model. methods_md() writes its equations. jsdgam() fits joint species distribution models. The overview vignette introduces the package. The data vignette sets out the data format. The forecast evaluation article scores and compares forecasts. The multivariate formula article fits several responses at once. The integrated distribution model article ties several observation families to one latent process.

Other model fitting: check_newdata(), jsdgam(), mvgam_data(), mvgam_formula(), mvgam_multiple(), pivot_detection_array(), pivot_species_matrix(), series_to_mvgam(), stancode.mvgam_formula(), update.mvgam()

Examples

# \dontrun{
# One count series with a smooth effect of a covariate x and an
# AR(1) latent trend, split into training and test times
set.seed(2)
simdat <- sim_mvgam(family = poisson(), n_timepoints = 100L,
                    trend_model = AR(), prop_trend = 0.5)
head(simdat$data_train)
#>    y   series time          x
#> 1  6 series_1    1 -1.2604710
#> 2  3 series_1    2  0.8094961
#> 3 19 series_1    3  0.2933053
#> 4  7 series_1    4 -1.3277923
#> 5  7 series_1    5  1.7753574
#> 6  4 series_1    6  1.7738998

# The parameters a model takes, with their default priors, before
# any fitting. A `prior` argument to mvgam() replaces any of them
get_prior(
  mvgam_formula(y ~ s(x), trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1)),
  data   = simdat$data_train,
  family = poisson()
)
#>                   prior       class coef group resp dpar nlpar lb ub tag
#>  student_t(3, 1.4, 2.5)   Intercept                                     
#>                  (flat)           b                                     
#>                  (flat)           b sx_1                                
#>    student_t(3, 0, 2.5)         sds                             0       
#>    student_t(3, 0, 2.5)         sds s(x)                        0       
#>          exponential(2) sigma_trend                             0       
#>          normal(0, 0.5)   ar1_trend                            -1  1    
#>        source
#>       default
#>       default
#>  (vectorized)
#>       default
#>  (vectorized)
#>       default
#>       default

# A smooth of x in the observation model and an AR(1) latent trend.
# The test data are stored on the fit for forecasting
mod <- mvgam(
  y ~ s(x),
  trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1),
  data          = simdat$data_train,
  newdata       = simdat$data_test,
  family        = poisson(),
  chains        = 2,
  silent        = 2
)
#> Warning: 21 of 2000 (1.0%) transitions ended with a divergence.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.
summary(mod)
#>  Family: poisson 
#>   Links: mu = log 
#> Formula: y ~ s(x) 
#>    Data: simdat$data_train (Number of observations: 75) 
#>  Trends: AR(1) 
#>   Draws: 2 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1; 
#>          total post-warmup draws = 2000
#> 
#> == Observation Model ==
#> Smoothing Spline Hyperparameters:
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> sds(sx_1)     9.68      4.02     2.87    19.38 1.00      232      216
#> 
#> Regression Coefficients:
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept     1.57      0.21     1.20     1.99 1.01      783      726
#> sx_1         -7.48      9.51   -26.65    10.01 1.00      377      822
#> 
#> == Trend Model ==
#> Trend Specific Parameters:
#>                       Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS
#> sigma_trend[series_1]     0.37      0.09     0.22     0.57 1.00      381
#> ar1_trend[series_1]       0.69      0.15     0.34     0.93 1.00      300
#>                       Tail_ESS
#> sigma_trend[series_1]      690
#> ar1_trend[series_1]        579
#> 
#> Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
#> and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
#> scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).
#> 
#> Next steps:
#>   - `pp_check(fit)`: posterior predictive checks
#>   - `forecast(fit, newdata = ...)`: out-of-sample forecasts

#> Use `how_to_cite(fit)` for a methods paragraph and `methods_md(fit)` for its equations.

# Do draws from the model resemble the observed counts?
pp_check(mod)


# The effect of x on the expected count
conditional_effects(mod)


# Forecasts of the test times, with the held-out counts overlaid
plot(forecast(mod))


# A methods paragraph with its references
how_to_cite(mod)
#> Methods text skeleton
#> We used the R package mvgam (version 2.0.0; Clark & Wells, 2023) to
#>   construct, fit and interrogate the model. mvgam fits Bayesian
#>   state-space models that combine flexible predictor effects in both the
#>   process and observation components, using functionality from the brms
#>   (Burkner 2017) and mgcv (Wood 2017) packages. The mvgam-constructed
#>   model and data were passed to Stan (Carpenter et al. 2017) via the
#>   cmdstanr interface (Gabry et al. 2024). We ran 2 Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
#>   chains for 1000 warmup iterations and 1000 sampling iterations.
#>   Rank-normalised split Rhat and effective sample sizes (Vehtari et al.
#>   2021) were used to monitor convergence.
